rows.description: A parent or carer strokes a child's back or an elder's hand to soothe. The receiver's comfort, not the giver's intention, decides whether it helps, so watch for relaxing breath or flinching.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: calm, relief from stress

rows.subtype: Comfort touch in grief and care [Interpreting]
rows.description: A young adult offers a hand on the shoulder or a hug to a grieving friend and watches for signs of acceptance. Touch can soothe but may not suit everyone; asking can I hug you respects choice and shows care.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: affection, admiration, grief

rows.subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
rows.description: A young professional shakes hands, offers a namaste or a nod according to setting, gender norms and health needs. A firm, brief handshake conveys respect, but preferences differ, so following the other person's lead is wise.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A young adult reads a delayed reply, a muted camera or a left-on-read message as distance. Such digital signals may mean busyness, tech trouble or coldness, and a direct kind question beats silent assumption.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A young professional reads who sits next to whom, who stands close to the boss and who keeps distance in meetings. Seating can reflect rank, habit or logistics; assuming a hidden meaning without evidence leads to misjudgment.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Laughing in meetings and difficult talks [Regulating]
rows.description: A young professional uses a light laugh to ease tension, or holds one back in a solemn moment. A chuckle can build rapport, but laughing at a colleague's concern or a serious issue can seem dismissive.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Laughing through hurt and gallows humour [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young adult laughs about stress, a mistake or a hard time as a coping tool. It can show resilience but sometimes hides pain; a friend who listens without assuming can tell which by gently asking how they really are.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Bawling after overwhelming loss or relief [Regulating]
rows.description: An adult may bawl during grief, shock or after long tension. Allowing it in a safe place, then drinking water, breathing slowly and reaching for support helps the body settle; suppressing it can prolong the strain.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: grief, surprise, relief, overwhelm

rows.subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
rows.description: A young professional tears up after harsh feedback or stress and tries to compose themselves. Norms differ across workplaces, so stepping out briefly, breathing and returning with a plan is reasonable, and peers should respond with kindness.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: sadness, relief from stress

rows.description: A young adult offers a tissue, quiet presence or a listening ear to a crying friend and avoids rushing them or saying stop. Not every cry needs fixing; asking what would help respects their control and signals real care.
